summary: Compare two fractions that share a numerator or a denominator by reasoning about the SIZE and COUNT of the parts, not the size of the digits. Same denominator: parts are equal-sized, so more of them is more (5/6 > 2/6). Same numerator: the same count of parts, but a larger denominator makes each part smaller, so the fraction is smaller (3/8 < 3/4). When comparing by shaded models, both fractions must be drawn on the SAME whole for the picture to be fair; comparisons are recorded with >, =, <.
misconceptions: Whole-number bias — a larger denominator means a larger fraction (1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3; 3/8 > 3/4 by comparing denominators) (IES)
Comparing across different wholes (3/4 of a small bar vs 1/2 of a large bar)
Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers
Over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' so blindly it mis-fires on same-denominator pairs

activities.title: Lock the numerator, grow the denominator: watch the parts shrink
steps: Set up two bars (strips, drawn area models, or an interactive tool) pinned to the SAME whole.
Set both bars to 3/4 to start (numerator 3 and denominator 4 on each), so the two shaded amounts are identical.
On the first bar, raise the denominator from 4 to 8 so it shows 3/8; keep the second at 3/4.
Describe what happens to each part as the bottom number grows from 4 to 8, then state which shaded amount is larger.
Write the correct symbol between them (3/8 __ 3/4) with the sign opening toward the larger amount.
Say aloud: 'Same number of parts (3), but each eighth is smaller than each fourth, so 3/8 is less than 3/4.'
activities.insight: When the numerator is held fixed, a larger denominator cuts the whole into more, smaller parts, so the fraction gets SMALLER, not bigger. The digits '8 > 4' do not mean '3/8 > 3/4'.

activities.title: Same denominator: count the equal parts
steps: On one whole, shade 5/6 and 2/6 on aligned bars or on a single 0–1 number line.
State that the sixths are all the same size on both.
Decide which is larger by counting how many equal parts are shaded, then write 5/6 __ 2/6.
Explain: 'Same-size sixths, and five of them is more than two, so 5/6 > 2/6.'
activities.insight: When the denominator is shared, the parts are identical in size, so the fraction with more parts (larger numerator) is larger. This is a DIFFERENT comparison from the same-numerator case and must not be solved by 'bigger bottom = smaller'.

activities.title: Does 3/4 always beat 3/8? The same-whole rule
steps: Draw 3/4 on a short bar and 3/8 on a long bar, deliberately mismatched.
Compare the shaded regions by eye and notice the drawing can be misleading.
Redraw both fractions on identical wholes and compare again.
State in your own words why, when you compare by shaded pictures, both fractions must be drawn on the same whole for the comparison to be fair.
activities.insight: When you judge which fraction is larger by looking at shaded regions, both must be drawn on the same whole for the picture to be fair; 3/4 of a small bar can look smaller than 3/8 of a large bar, even though, as numbers, 3/4 > 3/8.

activities.title: Practise and sort comparisons
steps: Decide the correct sign for same-numerator pairs (e.g. 3/8 vs 3/4) and same-denominator pairs (e.g. 5/6 vs 2/6).
Order short sets of same-numerator fractions and, separately, same-denominator fractions from smallest to largest.
Sort pairs into >, =, and < groups and, where used, match a fraction pair to its symbol.
For each answer, state the reason in part-size/count language rather than quoting digits.
activities.insight: Fluency in applying the two lines of reasoning across varied pairs, with the correct rule chosen for the structure of each pair.

activities.title: Reference fraction wall (support)
steps: Line up two rows of a fraction wall, e.g. place 3/8 under 3/4 on the same whole, to see relative sizes.
Use a lift-the-flap or note to recall 'eighths are smaller, so 3/8 is less than 3/4'.
Return to the drawing/building activities to test and justify an actual comparison.
activities.insight: A fraction wall helps recall relative sizes of common fractions as a reference aid.

checkQuestion: Task: using bars drawn on the same whole (or a number line), show which is larger and write >, <, or = — first for 3/8 and 3/4, then for 5/6 and 2/6. I'll watch how you build and decide each one.
checkAnswer: 3/8 < 3/4 (same number of parts, but eighths are smaller than fourths, so three eighths is less than three fourths); 5/6 > 2/6 (same-size sixths, and five of them is more than two). Both drawn on the same whole.
